Title: Heterogeneous Variational Inference for Markov Degradation Hazard Models: Discretized Mixture with Interpretable Clusters
Text:
Heterogeneous Variational Inference for Markov Degradation
Hazard Models: Discretized Mixture with Interpretable Clusters
Takato Yasuno1
1Digital Business Department, Yachiyo Engineering Co., Ltd.
Abstract
Infrastructure asset management requires under-
standing heterogeneous degradation patterns across
equipment to optimize maintenance decisions. Tra-
ditional survival analysis assumes homogeneous haz-
ard rates, failing to capture pump-specific degrada-
tion speeds that vary by 17× to 34× relative to the
population average in real-world industrial settings.
Challenge: Bayesian finite mixture models can
identify discrete risk clusters (low-risk vs. high-risk
equipment), but face three critical bottlenecks: (1)
insufficient degradation signals from coarse state dis-
cretization, (2) unstable cluster identification when
data inherently supports fewer clusters than explored,
and (3) computational infeasibility of Markov Chain
Monte Carlo (MCMC) methods for production de-
ployment (7+ hours per model).
Approach:
We propose a practical framework
combining (1) 8-state
global
percentile
dis-
cretization that amplifies degradation events by
+83% (1.3% →2.4% transition rate),
(2) 30-
dimensional feature engineering integrating sta-
tistical trends (22 features), continuous health in-
dicators, and text embeddings (PCA-compressed to
3 dimensions), (3) interpretable model selection
rules enforcing minimum cluster share (≥5%) and
separation (∆µ ≥0.15) alongside WAIC, and (4) Au-
tomatic Differentiation Variational Inference
(ADVI) with full-rank covariance for stable, fast es-
timation (5 minutes vs. 7h 40min for NUTS).
Validation:
Applied to 280 industrial pump
equipment with 104,703 inspection records (1991–
2025), we demonstrate: (1) Random effect models
(baseline) show ADVI and NUTS produce nearly
identical estimates (r > 0.99) with 15× speedup,
validating ADVI accuracy. (2) Finite mixture mod-
els identify optimal K = 2 clusters (72.9% low-risk,
27.1% high-risk, ∆µ = 0.98), with K = 3 failing in-
terpretability constraints (2.9% minimum share). (3)
NUTS exhibits severe convergence issues (ˆr = 1.19–
1.28 for µ parameters) and label switching, while
ADVI provides stable results in 84× less time.
Contributions: (1) First demonstration that fine-
grained state discretization (8-state) is essential for
mixture model stability in survival analysis.
(2)
Comprehensive feature engineering strategy combin-
ing statistical, continuous, and semantic (text) sig-
nals.
(3) Practical interpretability rules preventing
overfitting in automated model selection.
(4) Em-
pirical evidence that ADVI outperforms NUTS for
finite mixture models in terms of convergence, sta-
bility, and computational efficiency—challenging the
conventional wisdom that MCMC methods are always
superior.
Keywords: Automatic Differentiation Variational
Inference, Markov hazard models, Random Effect
Heterogeneity, Finite mixture clustering, Equipment
degradation, global percentile discretization, inter-
pretability rules, industrial asset management.

Introduction
1.1
Background and Motivation
Industrial infrastructure degradation poses critical
challenges for asset management.
Equipment such
as pumps, turbines, and compressors exhibit hetero-
geneous degradation patterns—individual units de-
grade at vastly different rates even under similar op-
erating conditions [1, 2]. Understanding this hetero-
geneity is essential for optimizing maintenance sched-
ules, preventing catastrophic failures, and allocating
limited budgets.
Traditional survival analysis models assume a ho-
mogeneous hazard rate across all equipment, mod-
eling degradation as a function of time and observ-
able covariates (age, usage intensity, environmental
factors) [3, 4].
However, real-world industrial data
reveals substantial individual-level variation: in our
pump equipment dataset, degradation speeds vary
from 34× slower to 17× faster than the population

1.2
Problem
Statement
and
Chal-
lenges
Despite their theoretical appeal, applying Bayesian
finite mixture models to degradation data faces three
critical challenges:
Challenge 1:
Insufficient degradation sig-
nals.
Equipment health is typically recorded as
continuous measurements (e.g., vibration amplitude,
temperature). Discretizing health into 4 coarse states
(Good/Normal/Caution/Degraded) for Markov mod-
eling yields only 1.3% degradation events in our
data—insufficient diversity for stable mixture cluster-
ing. Prior work has not systematically explored the
impact of state granularity on mixture model perfor-
mance.
Challenge 2:
Model selection instability.
Grid search over cluster numbers K ∈{2, 3, 4, 5} may
favor complex models (K = 5) with tiny, uninter-
pretable clusters (e.g., 2.9% share) when standard in-
formation criteria (WAIC, AIC) are used alone. Ex-
isting methods lack interpretability constraints to en-
sure clusters are meaningful for practitioners.
Challenge 3: Computational infeasibility of
MCMC. No-U-Turn Sampler (NUTS), the gold stan-
dard for Bayesian inference [7], requires approxi-
mately 7 hours 40 minutes per model in our appli-
cation. For grid search over K = 2–5 with 4 parallel
jobs, total execution exceeds 8 hours—impractical for
iterative model development. Moreover, finite mix-
ture models suffer from label switching where MCMC
chains explore equivalent cluster permutations, caus-
ing convergence failures [8].
1.3
Proposed Approach
We propose a comprehensive framework addressing
all three challenges:
Solution 1:
8-state global percentile dis-
cretization. Instead of 4 states, we partition equip-
ment health into 8 states using global percentiles
(12.5%, 25%, 37.5%, ..., 87.5%), ensuring balanced
state distributions (11.8%–13.1% per state). This am-
plifies degradation events from 1.3% to 2.4% (+83%
increase), providing richer transition patterns for mix-
ture clustering.
Solution 2:
Interpretable model selection
rules. Beyond WAIC minimization, we enforce three
constraints: (a) WAIC within tolerance (±50) of the
best model, (b) minimum cluster share ≥5% (ensur-
ing all clusters are meaningful), and (c) minimum sep-
aration ∆µ ≥0.15 between adjacent cluster means
(ensuring distinguishability).
These rules prevent
overfitting while maintaining practitioner trust.
Solution 3:
ADVI with full-rank covari-
ance.
Automatic Differentiation Variational Infer-
ence (ADVI) [9] approximates the posterior p(θ|D)
via optimization rather than sampling, reducing exe-
cution time from 7h 40min (NUTS) to 5 minutes—an
84× speedup.
We use full-rank ADVI (not mean-
field) to capture posterior correlations, critical for
mixture model stability.

2
Related Work
2.1
Survival
Analysis
and
Hazard
Models
Classical survival analysis originated with Cox’s pro-
portional hazards model [3], assuming a baseline haz-
ard λ0(t) modified by covariate effects:
λ(t|X) =
λ0(t) exp(βT X). While widely used in medical stud-
ies (patient survival) and reliability engineering (com-
ponent lifetime), the proportional hazards assump-
tion often fails in practice when equipment exhibits
time-varying effects or discrete state transitions.
Markov degradation models address this by parti-
tioning equipment health into K discrete states (e.g.,
Good, Normal, Caution, Degraded) and modeling
transitions as time-inhomogeneous Markov chains [4,
10].
The hazard rate λk→k+1(t) for transitioning
from state k to k + 1 depends on both state and co-
variates, capturing non-proportional degradation pat-
terns. However, most implementations assume homo-
geneous transition rates across equipment, ignoring
individual-level heterogeneity.
2.2
Bayesian Hierarchical Models for
Heterogeneity
Bayesian hierarchical (mixed-effects) models intro-
duce equipment-specific random effects ui ∼N(0, σ2
u)
to account for unobserved heterogeneity [1]. The log-
hazard becomes log λi(t) = log λ0(t) + βT Xi(t) + ui,
where ui represents pump i’s deviation from the pop-
ulation average.
Inference traditionally relies on Markov Chain
Monte Carlo (MCMC) methods, particularly Hamil-
tonian Monte Carlo (HMC) [11] and its adaptive vari-
ant No-U-Turn Sampler (NUTS) [7].
PyMC [12],
Stan [13], and JAGS [14] provide accessible imple-
mentations.
However, MCMC convergence can be
slow (hours to days) and diagnostics (ˆr, effective sam-
ple size) may indicate failures even after lengthy runs.

Analytical approaches to mixture Markov degra-

2.4
Variational Inference and ADVI
Variational inference (VI) approximates the poste-
rior p(θ|D) by optimizing a tractable distribution
q(θ) to minimize KL-divergence [19, 20]. Automatic
Differentiation Variational Inference (ADVI) [9] au-
tomates VI for arbitrary probabilistic programs by:
(1) transforming constrained parameters to uncon-
strained space, (2) assuming Gaussian variational
families (mean-field or full-rank), and (3) optimizing
via stochastic gradient descent. Rather than deriving
3


gradients analytically, ADVI exploits automatic dif-
ferentiation [21] to efficiently evaluate derivatives, en-
abling practitioners to focus on model design rather
than manual calculus—a key advantage for rapidly
obtaining degradation rankings and curves.
ADVI offers dramatic speedups (10×–1000×) over
MCMC but faces criticism for approximation er-
rors [22]. Mean-field ADVI assumes independent pos-
teriors q(θ) = Q
j q(θj), ignoring correlations. Full-
rank ADVI uses q(θ) = N(µ, Σ) with full covariance
Σ, capturing dependencies at higher computational
cost (still orders of magnitude faster than MCMC).
Recent work questions whether ADVI underper-
forms for complex models like mixtures.
Our em-
pirical investigation reveals the opposite: ADVI pro-
vides more stable results than NUTS for finite mix-
ture models, challenging conventional assumptions.
2.5
Infrastructure Degradation Mod-
eling
Prior work on infrastructure degradation focuses on
structural health monitoring (SHM) using sensor data
(vibration, strain, acoustic emission) [23, 24].
Ma-
chine learning approaches (neural networks, random
forests) predict failures from high-frequency sensor
streams [25]. However, most industrial facilities lack
continuous sensing, relying instead on periodic in-
spections (monthly to quarterly) with manual read-
ings—our data modality.
Discrete-state Markov models have been applied to
bridge deterioration [26], pavement cracking [27], and
pipeline corrosion [28], typically with 3–5 states. To
our knowledge, no prior work systematically explores
8-state discretization or integrates text embeddings
(inspection comments) into degradation models.

3.1
Problem
Formulation:
Markov
Degradation Hazard Model
Consider N equipment units (pumps) observed over
time through periodic inspections.
For each pump
i ∈{1, . . . , N}, we record a sequence of inspections
at times ti1, ti2, . . . , tini.
At each inspection j, we
observe:
• Health measurement yij ∈R: continuous in-
dicator (e.g., vibration amplitude, temperature)
• Covariates Xij ∈Rp:
time-varying features
(age, operational history, statistical trends)
• Time interval ∆tij = tij −ti,j−1: days since
previous inspection
To enable Markov modeling, we discretize the con-
tinuous health measurements into K ordered states
{1, 2, . . . , K} representing progressive degradation
(state 1 = healthiest, state K = most degraded). Let
sij ∈{1, . . . , K} denote the discrete state at inspec-
tion j for pump i.
The hazard rate λik(t) represents the instanta-
neous risk of transitioning from state k to state k + 1
for pump i at time t.
We model this via a log-
linear form capturing both population-level effects
and pump-specific heterogeneity:
log λik(t) = log λ0k + βT Xi(t) + ui
(2)
where:
• λ0k: baseline hazard for state k (shared across
all pumps)
• β ∈Rp: covariate effect coefficients (population-
level)
• ui: pump-specific random effect (unobserved het-
erogeneity)
The probability of transitioning from state si,j−1 at
time ti,j−1 to state sij > si,j−1 during interval ∆tij
follows an exponential survival model:
P(transition | si,j−1, Xij, ∆tij)
= 1 −exp(−λi,si,j−1 · ∆tij)
(3)
For stable equipment (no transition), the probabil-
ity is:
P(stable | si,j−1, Xij, ∆tij) = exp(−λi,si,j−1 · ∆tij)
(4)
This
formulation
captures
time-inhomogeneous
degradation where hazard rates vary across states and
evolve with time-varying covariates, while ui accounts
for pump-specific degradation speeds.

Discussion
5.1
Summary of Key Findings
Our comprehensive evaluation of Bayesian finite mix-
ture models for equipment degradation reveals four
critical insights:
Finding 1:
ADVI reliability for mixture
models. Full-rank ADVI achieves an 84× speedup
over NUTS (5 min vs. 7h 40min) while delivering su-
perior convergence stability for finite mixture models:
NUTS exhibits ˆr = 1.19–1.28 and ESS< 25 with la-
bel switching across chains, whereas ADVI converges
reliably with no divergences. For continuous random
effect baselines, both methods agree closely (r > 0.99,
RMSE= 0.038), confirming that the speedup does not
sacrifice accuracy.
These results establish full-rank
ADVI as the more reliable inference strategy for fi-
nite mixture degradation models (cf. Section 4).
Finding 2: State granularity is critical. In-
creasing state discretization from 4 coarse states to
8 fine-grained states (via global percentiles) ampli-
fies degradation signals by 83% (1.3% →2.4% event
rate). This increased diversity stabilizes mixture clus-
tering: 4-state discretization leads to empty clusters
for C = 3, while 8-state yields interpretable (albeit
failing min share rule) clusters. State granularity di-
rectly impacts model identifiability.
Finding 3: Interpretability constraints pre-
vent overfitting.
Standard information criteria
(WAIC) favor C = 3 over C = 2 (WAIC=19,814 vs.
19,788, ∆= 26), but C = 3 produces a 2.9% minor-
ity cluster—operationally unactionable.
Our three-
tier framework (WAIC tolerance, min share ≥5%,
min gap ≥0.15) prevents such overfitted models, en-
suring practitioner trust and deployment feasibility.
Finding 4: Feature engineering stabilizes but
cannot force unnatural clusterings. Expanding
from 7 basic features to 30 covariates (adding 22 sta-
tistical trends/volatility features) eliminates empty
clusters in C = 3, but the 2.9% minimum share still
fails interpretability. This confirms that feature en-
gineering enhances signal quality but respects inher-
ent data structure—industrial pump degradation nat-
urally exhibits 2 latent risk groups, not 3.
5.2
Comparison to Existing Methods
5.2.1
Survival Analysis Literature
Traditional Cox proportional hazards models [3] as-
sume homogeneous hazard rates across equipment, ig-
noring the 79.6% of pumps with significant individual-
level heterogeneity in our data. Bayesian hierarchi-
cal models [1] address this via continuous random ef-
fects, but provide limited actionability: maintenance
managers cannot translate 280 individual ui values
into discrete strategies. Our finite mixture approach
bridges this gap, clustering equipment into 2 inter-
pretable risk categories with 17.5× vs. 34× degrada-
tion speed differences.
5.2.2
Variational Inference Critiques
Recent work [22] questions ADVI accuracy for com-
plex models, citing mean-field approximation errors.
Our results demonstrate that full-rank ADVI (cap-
turing posterior correlations) provides near-exact es-
timates for random effect models (r
> 0.99 vs.
NUTS) and superior stability for mixture models
where NUTS fails to converge. The key distinction:
mean-field ADVI (independent posteriors) vs.
full-
rank ADVI (full covariance).
Practitioners should
prefer full-rank for mixture models despite 2× com-
putational cost (still 100× faster than NUTS).
5.2.3
Infrastructure Degradation Modeling
Prior work on bridge deterioration [26] and pavement
cracking [27] employs 3–5 discrete states with homo-
geneous transition matrices. Our contributions: (1)
pump-specific heterogeneity via random/mixture ef-
fects, (2) 8-state fine-grained discretization for richer
signals, (3) text embedding integration (inspection
comments), and (4) 30-dimensional feature engineer-
ing. To our knowledge, this is the first application
of Bayesian finite mixture models with 8 states and
semantic (text) features to equipment degradation.
5.3
Practical Implications for Asset
Management
5.3.1
Maintenance Strategy Differentiation
The optimal C = 2 model enables two-tier mainte-

This paper presents a comprehensive framework for

6.1
Key Contributions
1. Empirical validation of state granularity im-
pact. We demonstrate that 8-state global percentile
discretization amplifies degradation events by 83%
(1.3% →2.4%), stabilizing mixture model identifi-
cation. This is the first systematic study quantifying
the relationship between state granularity and mix-
ture model performance in survival analysis.
2. Comprehensive feature engineering strat-
egy. Our 30-dimensional covariate framework inte-
grates statistical trends (22 features over 90-day win-
dows), continuous health indicators, and semantic sig-
nals (text embeddings compressed via PCA). This
eliminates empty clusters and provides richer degra-

structure (2 clusters, not 3).
3. Interpretability-constrained model selec-
tion.
The three-tier framework (WAIC tolerance,
min share ≥5%, min gap ≥0.15) prevents overfitting

4. ADVI superiority over NUTS for mixture
models. Across 280 pumps and 104,703 inspection

for finite mixture models: NUTS failed to converge

vs. 7h 40min). Near-exact agreement for random ef-

the speedup does not sacrifice accuracy—establishing
ADVI as the default inference method for production
Bayesian degradation systems.

Closing Remarks
The transition from research prototypes to produc-
tion AI systems requires balancing theoretical rigor
with practical constraints: interpretability, compu-
tational efficiency, and convergence stability.
Our
framework demonstrates that Bayesian finite mixture
models—when designed with domain-informed con-
straints and powered by full-rank ADVI—can achieve

A central insight of this work is that computa-

tively correlated in this setting: ADVI’s 84× speedup
over NUTS reflects fundamental differences in op-
timization behavior for complex mixture posteriors,
not merely reduced sampling overhead. As Bayesian
methods are increasingly deployed in high-stakes en-
gineering domains (infrastructure, finance, health-
care), selecting inference algorithms that converge re-
liably under finite data is as important as theoretical
posterior guarantees.
In summary: Full-rank variational inference for
Markov degradation models is not only feasible but
empirically preferable to MCMC for finite mixture
models, combining 84× speedup with superior conver-
gence stability and interpretability. Full-rank ADVI
is therefore recommended as the default inference
method for finite mixture degradation models in pro-
